extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; theorists and policymakers interested in consent theory, natural rights, and the foundations/limits of government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for the origin, ends, forms, and legitimate limits of political society and legislative power grounded in individual consent and the law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning of political society depends on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of politic society depends upon the consent of the individuals, to join into, and make one society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individuals incorporate into a society they may set up any form of government they think fit. Peaceful foundations of government are to be understood as arising from voluntary consent rather than from paternal or divine right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to choose form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Who, when they are thus incorporated, might set up what form of government they thought fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities may choose democracy, oligarchy, monarchy, or mixed forms according to what the majority or community grants as the supreme (legislative) power. Early choices (e.g., monarchy) often reflect practical needs and habits rather than a permanent or divine entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit and express consent — possession/ enjoyment implies tacit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man, that hath any possessions, or enjoyment, of any part of the dominions of any government, doth thereby give his tacit consent, and is as far forth obliged to obedience to the laws of that government, during such enjoyment, as any one under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacit consent covers possession of land (whether hereditary or temporary), lodging, or travelling within a government's territory. Such obligation begins and ends with the period of enjoyment; by quitting the possession a person may withdraw that tacit consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express consent required for permanent membership/subjecthood
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can make any man ... a member of that commonwealth, a perpetual subject of that commonwealth; nothing can make any man so, but his actually entering into it by positive engagement, and express promise and compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Living under laws and enjoying protections is a local obligation while present, but does not make one a lasting member or subject; permanent allegiance requires explicit incorporation or compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children and posterity cannot be bound by ancestors' compacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever engagements or promises any one has made for himself, he is under the obligation of them, but cannot, by any compact whatsoever, bind his children or posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A child, upon reaching age, is as free as the father; ancestral acts cannot transfer natural liberty. Governments themselves act accordingly (e.g., citizenship/admission rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: When incorporating, possessions are annexed to society
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man, when he at first incorporates himself into any commonwealth, he, by his uniting himself thereunto, annexed also, and submits to the community, those possessions, which he has, or shall acquire, that do not already belong to any other government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be contradictory to enter society to secure property yet claim that one's land is exempt from the society's jurisdiction; holdings enjoyed under the community are subject to its laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief end of political society: preservation of property
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and chief end, therefore, of men’s uniting into commonwealths, and putting themselves under government, is the preservation of their property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property is understood broadly as 'lives, liberties and estates.' This end explains why men leave the state of nature and create government institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three defects of the state of nature that government must remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature there wants (1) an established, settled, known law; (2) a known and indifferent judge; (3) power to back and support the sentence when right, and to give it due execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deficiencies motivate individuals to authorize common laws, impartial adjudicators, and an executive power to execute judgments for secure enjoyment of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers given up on forming society — scope and allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature a man has (1) the power to do whatsoever he thinks fit for preservation of himself and others; (2) the power to punish crimes. Both are given up when he joins a society: the first is regulated by society's laws; the second is wholly given to the executive power of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals transfer limited authority to the legislative and executive to secure mutual safety, but only to the extent required for the public good; they do not give up more power than they originally had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power as the fundamental positive law
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and fundamental positive law of all commonwealths is the establishing of the legislative power; this legislative is not only the supreme power of the commonwealth, but sacred and unalterable in the hands where the community have once placed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the legislative properly sanctioned by the community can enact binding laws; no other body's edict has the force of law without that sanction. This establishes the centrality of the legislative authority chosen by consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on legislative power — bounded by public good and natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative ... is not, nor can possibly be absolutely arbitrary over the lives and fortunes of the people ... their power ... is limited to the public good of the society. It can never have a right to destroy, enslave, or designedly to impoverish the subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative authority derives from what individuals could consent to in the state of nature and must be exercised for preservation and public welfare. Legislatures must govern by established, promulgated standing laws, with impartial judges and use of force only for executing such laws or defending against foreign injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human laws must conform to the law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules that they make for other men’s actions, must, as well as their own and other men’s actions, be conformable to the law of nature, i.e. to the will of God ... fundamental law of nature being the preservation of mankind, no human sanction can be good, or valid against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural law (preservation of mankind) is an ultimate standard: positive laws contrary to it lack moral validity. Legislators are therefore bound by higher principles when creating statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of commonwealth defined by placement of supreme power
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole power of the community is in the majority, the form is a democracy; if in a few select men, an oligarchy; if in one man, a monarchy. The form of government depends upon where the legislative (supreme) power is placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities may compose mixed or compounded forms; the same community can reconstitute or change form when the supreme power reverts to them or is reallocated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/functional reasons for early monarchy (descriptive normative guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early societies generally pitched upon monarchy because the father's government habituated people to one ruler, monarchy is simple and obvious, and in infancy of commonwealths defense against foreign force made selecting a single capable military leader natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why early/common historical instances favor single rulers: ease, safety, low internal disputes, and focus on military leadership rather than a claim of paternal or divine entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary/local obedience vs permanent political membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to the laws of any country, living quietly, and enjoying privileges and protection under them, makes not a man a member of that society; this is only a local protection and homage due to those within the territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreigners who live under another government's protection are bound to obey while enjoying it but are not thereby permanent members; actual membership requires positive engagement and express compact.
